column5: Recurring seasons and harvest
column6: The commentary treats pasture as the land’s recurring annual yield; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will continue while the earth remains, giving that cycle a covenant frame.

column5: Rain before field produce
column6: The commentary notes that the pasture clause itself omits rain; the immediately preceding verse promises rain in its seasons so Israel can gather grain, wine, and oil, supplying the source and agricultural continuation beside the grass-for-livestock verse.

column5: Hebrew מַרְעִיתוֹ, flock of his pasture
column6: The commentary labels Arabic merʿā with root r-ʿ-y and says it can name pasture as well as grazing; this psalm uses a cognate Hebrew pasture noun for God’s flock, joining the grazing ground to the creatures that depend on it.

column5: Wilderness changed to pools and springs
column6: The commentary describes pasture appearing in dry, uneven ground as a distinct gift; the psalm says God turns wilderness into pools and parched land into springs, a direct reversal from barrenness to life-sustaining water.

column5: Fields sown for fruitful yield
column6: The commentary calls pasture the earth’s yield and connects it to the survival of households; the psalm’s hungry settlers sow fields and plant vineyards that produce fruit, extending divine restoration into human cultivation and livelihood.

column5: God dries the green tree and makes the dry flourish
column6: The commentary follows pasture from green growth into dark debris; Ezekiel puts both reversals under God’s hand, who can dry a green tree and make a dry tree flourish, making divine control of both sides of the cycle explicit.

column5: Water on dry land and spirit on descendants
column6: The commentary reads pasture as new life brought out of hidden ground and points to resurrection; Isaiah promises water on thirsty land and God’s spirit on descendants, joining soil’s renewal to the renewal of a people.

column5: Descendants sprout among grass by streams
column6: The commentary connects pasture’s emergence with a later spiritual and human emergence; Isaiah pictures descendants sprouting among grass like willows beside flowing water, giving the same water-fed growth an explicit communal meaning.

column5: Righteousness and praise spring up like a garden
column6: The commentary makes the Lord’s pasture-making the ground for praise and connects plant emergence with moral instruction; Isaiah says God makes righteousness and praise spring up before the nations like earth’s growth and a garden’s seed, joining vegetation to public praise.

column5: Wilderness pastures turn green again
column6: The commentary presents the green pasture as a gift that may later wither; Joel addresses the animals and says the wilderness pastures become green and the trees bear fruit after devastation, making restored pasture a concrete sign of recovery.

column5: Sowing righteousness until rain comes
column6: The commentary develops pasture’s yield into a lesson about what sustains life and what endures; Hosea commands the people to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, break fallow ground, and seek God until he rains righteousness upon them, turning cultivation into an ethical summons.

column5: A tithe of the land’s yield belongs to God
column6: The commentary says the pasture arrives without a fee yet connects produce with a due given at harvest; Leviticus declares the tithe of seed and tree fruit holy to the Lord, adding a distinct claim of divine ownership over the yield.

column5: God’s word sustains beyond crop production
column6: The commentary places the Lord’s pasture provision beside the recited word; Wisdom says the manna teaches that crops themselves do not sustain people apart from God’s word, a precise Jewish reflection on food and divine speech.

column5: Blessing on seeing blossoming trees
column6: The commentary moves from visible new growth to glorifying its giver; the Talmud prescribes a blessing when one sees trees budding in Nisan, thanking God for a world that lacks nothing and for good trees made for human enjoyment.

column5: Field flowers grow without human toil
column6: The commentary says that grass emerges by the Lord’s action and is received without payment; Jesus points to lilies growing without labor or spinning as evidence of God’s care, making unworked growth a concrete sign of provision.

column5: Rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness
column6: The commentary identifies the Lord through pasture and says its yield is freely given; Paul tells his hearers that God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness, a compact Christian witness to the same provision chain.

column5: Seed, bread, and a harvest of righteousness
column6: The commentary connects annual yield with a duty to give from what the land produces; Paul says God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, then multiplies seed and the harvest of righteousness, joining provision to generosity.

column5: Called out of darkness into light
column6: The commentary reads vegetation’s emergence from hidden soil as an image for people brought from ignorance into light through scripture; Peter describes God calling a people out of darkness into marvelous light, giving that extraction image a communal and instructional form.

column5: Light shines from darkness into hearts
column6: The commentary compares a shoot emerging from dark soil with people brought from darkness to light by teaching; Paul invokes the Creator’s command that light shine from darkness and applies it to knowledge shining in human hearts, connecting creation speech with inward illumination.

column5: Grain dies and bears much fruit
column6: The commentary treats the pasture’s passage from life to decay as a sign that death need not be the final state; Jesus says a grain falling into the earth must die to bear much fruit, using the plant’s death as a distinct Christian account of life emerging through death.

column5: Seed decays and rises to bear fruit
column6: The commentary uses the pasture’s emergence and later decay to make resurrection imaginable; Clement describes dry seed falling into the earth and decaying before the Lord’s providence raises it into many fruitful plants, an explicit early Christian reading of vegetation as resurrection evidence.

column5: Uneven yields from different ground
column6: The commentary pictures green pasture appearing patchily, with bare earth beside it; in Jesus’ sower parable the seed falls on good soil and yields at different rates, a specific agricultural image of uneven ground and growth.

column5: The flock’s milk supports its keeper
column6: The commentary traces pasture from grass to the herd and then to human livelihood through milk, wool, and work; Paul asks whether a shepherd tends a flock without sharing its milk, making the animal-to-human support chain explicit in an argument about labor.

column5: The farmer waits for fruit and seasonal rains
column6: The commentary links the plant’s temporary cycle with the later judgment and what endures; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth’s precious fruit until the early and late rains, turning the crop cycle into a picture of eschatological patience.

column5: The earth’s ripe harvest at judgment
column6: The commentary places pasture’s short-lived growth before the surah’s final warnings; Revelation depicts the earth’s harvest as ripe and ready for reaping, giving agricultural growth an explicit end-time judgment image.

column5: Different measures of fruit from good soil
column6: The commentary stresses that vegetation appears in patches rather than as a uniform carpet; Jesus interprets the good soil as yielding thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold, making variation in the fruit of receptive ground explicit.

column5: Human life like field grass
column6: The commentary follows pasture’s brief green phase into decay and relates that passing life to the Hereafter; Isaiah calls all flesh grass and its glory a field flower, explicitly extending the vegetation image to human transience.

column5: New birth from imperishable seed through the word
column6: The commentary links plant emergence to human learning and then contrasts fading grass with retained recitation; Peter says believers are born again from imperishable seed through the living word, directly joining agricultural generation to enduring proclamation.

column5: Hidden things brought to light
column6: The commentary says pasture comes from an unseen place and connects emergence with God’s knowledge of what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the heart’s purposes, giving that hidden-to-manifest relation an ethical and eschatological use.
